question: In the study comparing mobile SMBG technology and family-centered goal setting for adolescents with type 1 diabetes, what was the HbA1c reduction at 3 months for the combined approach?
passage_1: Advancing Diabetes Management in Adolescents: Comparative Effectiveness of Mobile Self-Monitoring Blood Glucose Technology and Family-Centered Goal Setting evaluates three strategies—a health information technology (HIT)-enhanced blood glucose meter that shares real-time data and allows text messaging, a clinic-based family-centered goal setting intervention using motivational interviewing, and a combined approach of both—to improve self-monitoring of blood glucose (SMBG) and glycemic control (HbA1c) in adolescents aged 12–18 with type 1 diabetes over a 6-month period. The study found that HIT-enhanced SMBG alone resulted in no change in mean HbA1c, family-centered goal setting showed a non-significant decrease of 0.3% at 6 months, and the combined approach demonstrated a significant HbA1c reduction of 0.6% at 3 months that diminished to a non-significant 0.4% reduction by 6 months, with higher baseline HbA1c levels predicting greater improvement; additionally, there were no significant changes or group differences in the daily frequency of SMBG testing. Based on these findings, the authors recommend further research into pairing family-centered goal setting with HIT-enhanced diabetes technologies, noting that family goal setting and counseling may be particularly useful when adolescents adopt new self-management technologies to achieve optimal clinical outcomes, especially among those with higher baseline HbA1c levels.

The findings revealed no overall significant differences in A1C across the three groups at the end of two years, and monthly outreach alone provided no added benefit over standard care when regular quarterly clinic visits were maintained; however, a subgroup analysis of youth with suboptimal baseline control (A1C ≥ 8%) showed that the psychoeducational intervention significantly helped maintain or improve A1C levels (77% vs. 52%) and sustain parent involvement (36% vs. 11%) compared to the combined non-psychoeducation groups, all without increasing diabetes-specific family conflict or decreasing youth quality of life. question: In the cohort sequential study on decision-making involvement in youth with type 1 diabetes, which child-reported subscales peaked around ages 12–14 before declining?
passage_1: The study Decision-Making Involvement and Prediction of Adherence in Youth With Type 1 Diabetes: A Cohort Sequential Study evaluates developmental trajectories of decision-making involvement (DMI)—defined as the ways in which parents and children engage each other regarding T1D management—and examines how DMI impacts adherence levels and age-related changes over time in youth aged 8 to 16 assessed five times over two years. Findings revealed that most DMI aspects increased with age, though certain child-reported subscales (Parent Express, Child Seek, and Joint) peaked around ages 12–14 before declining; additionally, higher levels of Child Seek, Child Express, and Joint behaviors were significantly associated with higher overall treatment adherence in both parent and youth reports, though DMI did not significantly alter the rate of adherence decline over time. Recommendations and guidelines suggest targeting interventions toward encouraging proactive child participation in T1D discussions—specifically coaching youth to share information, express opinions, and solicit parental guidance—to support effective self-management as children transition toward greater autonomy.
passage_2: The study Glycemic control and complications in patients with type 1 diabetes – a registry-based longitudinal study of adolescents and young adults evaluates longitudinal glycemic control, the prevalence of microvascular complications (retinopathy and nephropathy), and the impact of transition timing from pediatric to adult care among 874 young people with type 1 diabetes in Norway using data linked from two nationwide registries. The study found that median HbA1c peaked in late adolescence at 9.3% for females at age 17 and 9.1% for males at age 19, with overall target HbA1c levels achieved by very few participants (only 11% of adolescents aged 14–17 and 7% of young adults aged 18–25). Microvascular complications were prevalent, with 16% of participants exhibiting retinopathy and 13% exhibiting nephropathy; higher HbA1c levels across adolescence and young adulthood, longer diabetes duration, younger age at diagnosis, and smoking were strongly associated with a higher risk of complications. Additionally, patients who transferred to adult care before age 18 had significantly higher HbA1c levels and a higher prevalence of complications than those who transferred between ages 18–22, while less than 40% of patients with albuminuria were receiving recommended ACE inhibitor or ARB treatment. Based on these findings, the paper recommends that pediatricians and endocrinologists critically assess the care offered to adolescents and young adults, adopt new approaches to help improve glycemic control during the vulnerable late-teen years, optimize transition strategies to adult care, and strictly adhere to clinical guidelines regarding blood pressure and kidney protection medications for patients with nephropathy.

Findings indicate that 80% of caregivers and 66% of adolescents logged into a decision aid at least once, spending an average of 55.0 and 46.2 minutes on the website and viewing 72.2% and 77.4% of the content, respectively. Bivariate and regression analyses revealed that non-Hispanic, Caucasian females from higher socioeconomic status households were significantly more likely to log in, while adolescent males with lower health literacy demonstrated fewer logins. Based on these results, the paper recommends that future shared decision-making trials seek to actively promote decision aid engagement—particularly among non-White adolescents, potentially via direct assistance during the initial login—and explicitly guidelines that trials employing electronic decision aids routinely measure, report, and analyze objective utilization data.

question: In the SEARCH for Diabetes in Youth Study, what was the prevalence of disordered eating behaviors in youth with type 1 diabetes versus type 2 diabetes receiving insulin therapy?
passage_1: Disordered Eating Behaviors in Youth and Young Adults With Type 1 or Type 2 Diabetes Receiving Insulin Therapy:The SEARCH for Diabetes in Youth Study evaluates the prevalence of disordered eating behaviors (DEB) and their associations with glycemic control, insulin sensitivity, and psychosocial functioning in youth and young adults with type 1 or type 2 diabetes receiving insulin therapy. Analyzing a cohort of 2,156 participants with type 1 diabetes and 149 participants with type 2 diabetes using the Diabetes Eating Problem Survey–Revised (DEPS-R), the study found that DEB was present in 21.2% of individuals with type 1 diabetes and 50.3% of those with type 2 diabetes. Across both diabetes types, participants experiencing DEB demonstrated higher BMI z scores, lower insulin sensitivity, increased depressive symptoms, and a lower quality of life compared to those without DEB, with diabetic ketoacidosis episodes occurring significantly more often in type 1 diabetes participants with DEB. Based on these findings, the paper recommends heightened clinical awareness and early interventions tailored to address disordered eating in this vulnerable population, alongside calling for future longitudinal studies to track the long-term trajectory of DEB and its impact on diabetes outcomes.
passage_2: The systematic review Screening and identification of disordered eating in people with type 1 diabetes: A systematic review evaluates the reliability, validity, and clinical utility of 48 individual tools used to screen or identify disordered eating behaviors and eating disorders in individuals with Type 1 Diabetes across 90 studies. The authors found that the overall quality of the reported tools was poor, with a high risk of bias stemming from the widespread use of non-validated assessment tools and a lack of comparison against the reference standard of a diagnostic clinical interview. While the review notes that current guidelines suggest routine screening for disordered eating in people with Type 1 Diabetes due to elevated risk and associated health complications, it highlights a critical lack of evidence regarding which specific tools are most valid and reliable across different age groups and clinical settings. Consequently, the authors recommend that future research focus on evaluating the validity and reliability of available screening tools by directly comparing them against gold-standard diagnostic interviews to help establish standardized screening guidelines and improve clinical outcomes.
passage_3: The changing face of diabetes in youth: lessons learned from studies of type 2 diabetes evaluates multicenter clinical and epidemiological studies—including TODAY, SEARCH, and HEALTHY—to examine the epidemiology, pathophysiology, diagnosis, treatment, and complications of type 2 diabetes in youth. Findings demonstrate that youth-onset type 2 diabetes is characterized by severe insulin resistance and a rapid decline in pancreatic β-cell function that progresses three to four times faster than in adults, leading to significantly higher therapeutic failure rates with standard metformin treatment. The disease disproportionately affects minority racial and ethnic groups as well as female adolescents, with rising pediatric obesity clouding the clinical distinction between obese type 1 diabetes and type 2 diabetes. To address this growing health crisis, the authors highlight guidelines and recommendations for urgent development of novel, approved pharmacotherapeutic agents that target pediatric pathophysiological mechanisms alongside aggressive lifestyle and community-based prevention initiatives to halt the projected fourfold increase in youth type 2 diabetes by 2050.

question: In the study on early initiation of diabetes devices in children with recent-onset type 1 diabetes, what were the insulin pump and CGM usage rates at baseline and 6-month follow-up?
passage_1: Early Initiation of Diabetes Devices Relates to Improved Glycemic Control in Children with Recent-Onset Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus evaluates whether initiating an insulin pump or a continuous glucose monitor (CGM) within the first year of diagnosis is associated with reduced glycated hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c) levels in a cohort of 111 children aged 5 to 9 years with recent-onset type 1 diabetes. Tracking participants from baseline (mean diabetes duration of 4.7 months) to a 6-month follow-up (~12 months post-diagnosis), the study found that insulin pump usage grew from 17% to 35.1% and CGM usage increased from 17.1% to 25.2%. The findings demonstrate that children using an insulin pump maintained lower overall HbA1c levels compared to non-users, and children who started using a CGM during this timeframe experienced significantly lower HbA1c levels than those who did not. Based on these findings, the authors conclude and recommend that early initiation of either an insulin pump or a CGM in newly diagnosed children can help improve glycemic control within their first year of living with type 1 diabetes.
passage_2: The study Treatment regimens and glycaemic outcomes in more than 100 000 children with type 1 diabetes (2013–22): a longitudinal analysis of data from paediatric diabetes registries evaluates temporal trends in HbA1c levels, treatment modalities, and acute complications across international paediatric diabetes registries from 2013 to 2022. Between 2013 and 2022, aggregate mean HbA1c dropped from 8.2% to 7.6%, and the proportion of children reaching an HbA1c target below 7% increased from 19.0% to 38.8%, alongside marked increases in insulin pump usage (42.9% to 60.2%) and continuous glucose monitoring uptake (18.7% in 2016 to 81.7% in 2022). Concurrently, event rates per 100 person-years declined for both severe hypoglycaemia (from 3.0 to 1.7) and diabetic ketoacidosis (from 3.1 to 2.2). Despite these improvements coinciding with increased adoption of diabetes technology, many children still fail to achieve current International Society for Pediatric and Adolescent Diabetes (ISPAD) glycaemic targets, indicating that further advances in management are required even for youth with access to specialized care and technology.
passage_3: The SWEET Project 10-Year Benchmarking study evaluates time trends of key quality indicators and the impact of treatment changes in 16,082 youth with type 1 diabetes across 22 centers in 19 countries between 2008–2010 and 2016–2018. Over the 10-year period, adjusted mean HbA1c significantly improved from 68 mmol/mol (8.4%) to 63 mmol/mol (7.9%), coinciding with an increase in insulin pump use from 25.7% to 41.8% and continuous glucose monitoring sensor use from 1.5% to 44.6%. The percentage of patients achieving the target HbA1c of <7% (<53 mmol/mol) rose from 21% in 2008 to 34% in 2018, while severe hypoglycemia rates dropped from 3.8% to 2.4%, and secondary cardiovascular risk factors such as BMI-standard deviation score improved. The findings suggest that twice-yearly international benchmarking, standardized quality control, continuous data monitoring, and the adoption of modern diabetes technologies within centers of reference are effective strategies for improving long-term metabolic outcomes in pediatric type 1 diabetes care.

The study found that the ECRES algorithm calculated a significantly lower median carbohydrate intake overall compared to the tabular approach (13.5 g vs. 23.0 g; P < .01), which was particularly marked in physically active participants (9.0 g vs. 23.0 g; P < .01), while both methods successfully prevented hypoglycemia during exercise; post-exercise, ECRES maintained continuous glucose monitoring metrics within recommended target guidelines, whereas the tabular method resulted in significantly higher time below range in the afternoon (11.8% vs. target <4%; P < .05) and time above range during the night (39.3% vs. target <25%; P < .05).
passage_2: Effect of Continuous Glucose Monitoring on Glycemic Control in Adolescents and Young Adults With Type 1 Diabetes: A Randomized Clinical Trial evaluates the impact of continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) compared with standard blood glucose monitoring (BGM) on glycemic control over 26 weeks in 153 adolescents and young adults aged 14 to 24 years with type 1 diabetes. The study found that treatment with CGM resulted in a statistically significant reduction in mean HbA1c levels from 8.9% at baseline to 8.5% at 26 weeks, compared to remaining unchanged at 8.9% in the BGM group (an adjusted between-group difference of -0.37%). Additionally, participants in the CGM group demonstrated improvements in secondary outcomes, including time spent in the target glucose range and reduced daytime and nighttime glucose variability. The study concludes that CGM leads to small but statistically significant improvements in glycemic control in this population and notes that further research is needed to determine the clinical importance and long-term implications of these findings.
passage_3: The SWEET Project 10-Year Benchmarking study evaluates time trends of key quality indicators and the impact of treatment changes in 16,082 youth with type 1 diabetes across 22 centers in 19 countries between 2008–2010 and 2016–2018. The findings suggest that twice-yearly international benchmarking, standardized quality control, continuous data monitoring, and the adoption of modern diabetes technologies within centers of reference are effective strategies for improving long-term metabolic outcomes in pediatric type 1 diabetes care.

question: What demographic and clinical differences at diagnosis were found among African American youth with recent-onset type 1 diabetes compared to non-Hispanic white youth?
passage_1: Racial/Ethnic Minority Youth With Recent-Onset Type 1 Diabetes Have Poor Prognostic Factors evaluates the demographic and clinical differences at type 1 diabetes diagnosis and during the first three years post-diagnosis among non-Hispanic white, Hispanic, and African American youth under 19 years of age to understand variations in long-term health outcomes. The findings reveal that African American participants presented with higher BMI percentiles, more advanced pubertal development, a higher frequency of diabetic ketoacidosis at diagnosis, and higher rates of hypertension and severe hypoglycemia over the three-year follow-up, while being less likely to enter partial remission. Additionally, both Hispanic and African American youth maintained trajectories with higher insulin doses, higher IDAA1c, and higher BMI percentiles compared to non-Hispanic white youth, with Hispanics also demonstrating a higher prevalence of dyslipidemia.

The study finds that if 2017 incidence levels remain constant, youth diabetes cases will increase from 213,000 in 2017 (185,000 type 1; 28,000 type 2) to 239,000 in 2060 (191,000 type 1; 48,000 type 2), reflecting a 3% relative rise for type 1 and a 69% relative rise for type 2 diabetes. However, if the increasing incidence trends observed between 2002 and 2017 persist, total youth diabetes cases are projected to reach 526,000 by 2060 (306,000 type 1; 220,000 type 2)—representing a 65% relative increase for type 1 and a 673% relative increase for type 2 diabetes—with substantial widening of racial and ethnic disparities leading to the highest prevalence among non-Hispanic Black youth. Based on these projections, the paper highlights the urgent need for targeted prevention strategies to attenuate the rising burden of youth diabetes in future decades.

Findings demonstrate that youth-onset type 2 diabetes is characterized by severe insulin resistance and a rapid decline in pancreatic β-cell function that progresses three to four times faster than in adults, leading to significantly higher therapeutic failure rates with standard metformin treatment. The disease disproportionately affects minority racial and ethnic groups as well as female adolescents, with rising pediatric obesity clouding the clinical distinction between obese type 1 diabetes and type 2 diabetes. To address this growing health crisis, the authors highlight guidelines and recommendations for urgent development of novel, approved pharmacotherapeutic agents that target pediatric pathophysiological mechanisms alongside aggressive lifestyle and community-based prevention initiatives to halt the projected fourfold increase in youth type 2 diabetes by 2050.

question: What were the sensitivity and specificity of the American Diabetes Association risk-based screening criteria for detecting hyperglycemia in US youth aged 10–19 years?
passage_1: Screening and Diagnosis of Prediabetes and Diabetes in US Children and Adolescents evaluates the performance of American Diabetes Association risk-based screening criteria and current clinical definitions of prediabetes and diabetes—based on HbA1c, fasting plasma glucose (FPG), or both—to identify high cardiometabolic risk in US youth aged 10 to 19 years. The study found that while 25.5% of US youth met screening criteria, the sensitivity and specificity of these criteria were low for detecting hyperglycemia. Confirmed undiagnosed diabetes was rare (less than 0.5% of youth), with over 85% of diabetes cases already diagnosed. Furthermore, HbA1c-defined hyperglycemia showed significantly stronger and more specific associations with cardiometabolic risk compared to FPG-defined hyperglycemia. Based on these findings, the study highlights HbA1c as a highly specific, effective nonfasting test to identify high-risk youth who could benefit from lifestyle interventions to prevent diabetes and cardiovascular risks later in life.
passage_2: The Diabetes Screening With Hemoglobin A1c Versus Fasting Plasma Glucose in a Multiethnic Middle-School Cohort evaluates middle-school students with glycemic abnormalities by comparing high-risk hemoglobin A1c (hrA1C: 5.7–6.4%) with impaired fasting glucose (IFG: 100–125 mg/dL) to characterize their distribution, durability, and association with other diabetes risk factors. In this multiethnic 6th-grade cohort of 3,980 students, IFG was five times more common than hrA1C (16.0% vs. 3.2%), but hrA1C was more persistent over a two-year period into 8th grade (59.4% vs. 46.9%). High-risk A1C was strongly associated with non-Hispanic Black race/ethnicity, family history of diabetes, higher BMI, waist circumference, and fasting insulin, whereas IFG was associated with Hispanic ethnicity, male sex, higher BMI, waist circumference, fasting insulin, high blood pressure, and mean triglycerides. Over the 2-year study, very few children developed diabetes thresholds (0.8% with hrA1C developed A1C ≥6.5%, and 1.1% with IFG developed FPG ≥126 mg/dL), and only 58% of those identified with diabetes in 8th grade had previous baseline abnormalities. The study notes that optimal screening strategies and guidelines for diabetes in youth remain unresolved due to the modest predictive value of both measures and differing risk profiles.

It finds that type 1 diabetes is characterized by autoimmune beta-cell destruction leading to lifelong insulin dependence, affecting millions globally with substantial age-related and geographic variation in incidence. The study recommends recognizing clinical presentation variations between youth and adults, utilizing pancreatic autoantibody panels to differentiate type 1 from type 2 diabetes, and establishing early, structured transition plans from pediatric to adult clinical care teams. Additionally, guidelines provided in the paper outline standardized diagnostic criteria—such as fasting plasma glucose and A1C thresholds—alongside scheduled protocols for initial, quarterly, and annual evaluations covering microvascular and macrovascular complication screenings, autoimmune comorbidity checks, and individualized self-management support across all developmental stages.

question: Across the 20 studies in the systematic review on diabetes family conflict in young people with type 1 diabetes, how many found a significant association between greater family conflict and higher HbA1c values?
passage_1: The study "Systematic Review: Diabetes Family Conflict in Young People With Type 1 Diabetes" evaluates the relationships between diabetes-specific family conflict and various health outcomes—including glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c), treatment adherence, blood glucose monitoring, depression, anxiety, quality of life, and well-being—among young people with type 1 diabetes aged 14 to 25 years. Across 20 included studies, greater diabetes-specific family conflict was significantly associated with higher HbA1c values in 17 studies, suboptimal treatment adherence or less frequent blood glucose monitoring in 7 studies, and poorer quality of life, reduced well-being, or heightened depressive and anxiety symptoms in 7 studies, though 4 studies found no significant links to HbA1c or adherence. Given these findings, the authors recommend routine screening for and intervention addressing diabetes-specific family conflict in clinical practice, while highlighting guidelines for future research to prioritize longitudinal studies specifically targeting young people over the age of 16.
passage_2: Family-based Psychoeducation and Care Ambassador Intervention to Improve Glycemic Control in Youth with Type 1 Diabetes: A Randomized Trial evaluates the impact of a 2-year randomized clinical trial testing three levels of care—standard care with basic care coordination, monthly outreach by a Care Ambassador (CA), and monthly CA outreach plus quarterly family-based psychoeducation—on glycemic control (A1C), parental involvement, family conflict, and quality of life among 153 youth with type 1 diabetes. The findings revealed no overall significant differences in A1C across the three groups at the end of two years, and monthly outreach alone provided no added benefit over standard care when regular quarterly clinic visits were maintained; however, a subgroup analysis of youth with suboptimal baseline control (A1C ≥ 8%) showed that the psychoeducational intervention significantly helped maintain or improve A1C levels (77% vs. 52%) and sustain parent involvement (36% vs. 11%) compared to the combined non-psychoeducation groups, all without increasing diabetes-specific family conflict or decreasing youth quality of life. Based on these findings, the authors implicitly recommend incorporating structured psychoeducational strategies—focused on teamwork, setting realistic expectations, and joint problem-solving—alongside routine care coordination specifically for youth with suboptimal glycemic control, while cautioning against relying solely on frequent phone or email outreach without targeted behavioral support
passage_3: The Hvidoere Childhood Diabetes Study Group Centre Differences Study 2005 evaluates the glycaemic targets set by diabetes teams, how these targets are perceived by adolescents with type 1 diabetes and their parents, and their overall influence on metabolic control across 21 international centres. In an assessment of 2,062 adolescents, the study found a mean HbA1c of 8.2%, with significant variation between centres ranging from 7.4% to 9.1%. Key findings revealed a significant positive correlation between the HbA1c levels that adolescents and parents reported they would be happy with—as well as their perceived ideal targets—and their actual HbA1c results, with lower target HbA1c setting and greater consistency among multidisciplinary team members directly associating with lower overall centre HbA1c levels. Ultimately, the paper concludes that target setting plays a significant role in driving the metabolic differences observed across centres, demonstrating that clear and consistent setting of glycaemic targets by pediatric diabetes teams strongly improves HbA1c outcomes.

The percentage of patients achieving the target HbA1c of <7% (<53 mmol/mol) rose from 21% in 2008 to 34% in 2018, while severe hypoglycemia rates dropped from 3.8% to 2.4%, and secondary cardiovascular risk factors such as BMI-standard deviation score improved. The findings suggest that twice-yearly international benchmarking, standardized quality control, continuous data monitoring, and the adoption of modern diabetes technologies within centers of reference are effective strategies for improving long-term metabolic outcomes in pediatric type 1 diabetes care.

question: In the TODAY2 study of young adults with youth-onset type 2 diabetes, what percentage reported high overall diabetes distress, and what factors were significantly associated with high distress?
passage_1: The TODAY2 study evaluates the prevalence and associated factors of high diabetes distress among young adults with youth-onset type 2 diabetes. Analyzing 438 participants, the researchers found that 24% reported high overall diabetes distress, with 40% experiencing high regimen distress and 29.7% experiencing high emotional burden. High distress was significantly associated with female sex, higher HbA1c levels, moderate-to-severe anxiety symptoms, and a lack of healthcare coverage, while moderate-to-severe depressive symptoms were linked to both regimen distress and emotional burden, and insulin treatment was specifically linked to emotional burden. The paper recommends that future research focus on identifying modifiable factors associated with high diabetes distress in order to inform targeted psychosocial interventions for this medically vulnerable group.

Across 20 included studies, greater diabetes-specific family conflict was significantly associated with higher HbA1c values in 17 studies, suboptimal treatment adherence or less frequent blood glucose monitoring in 7 studies, and poorer quality of life, reduced well-being, or heightened depressive and anxiety symptoms in 7 studies, though 4 studies found no significant links to HbA1c or adherence. Given these findings, the authors recommend routine screening for and intervention addressing diabetes-specific family conflict in clinical practice, while highlighting guidelines for future research to prioritize longitudinal studies specifically targeting young people over the age of 16.

question: In the study on advancing diabetes management in adolescents, what was the effect of HIT-enhanced SMBG alone on mean HbA1c over 6 months?
passage_1: Effect of Continuous Glucose Monitoring on Glycemic Control in Adolescents and Young Adults With Type 1 Diabetes: A Randomized Clinical Trial evaluates the impact of continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) compared with standard blood glucose monitoring (BGM) on glycemic control over 26 weeks in 153 adolescents and young adults aged 14 to 24 years with type 1 diabetes. The study found that treatment with CGM resulted in a statistically significant reduction in mean HbA1c levels from 8.9% at baseline to 8.5% at 26 weeks, compared to remaining unchanged at 8.9% in the BGM group (an adjusted between-group difference of -0.37%). Additionally, participants in the CGM group demonstrated improvements in secondary outcomes, including time spent in the target glucose range and reduced daytime and nighttime glucose variability. The study concludes that CGM leads to small but statistically significant improvements in glycemic control in this population and notes that further research is needed to determine the clinical importance and long-term implications of these findings.
passage_2: Early Initiation of Diabetes Devices Relates to Improved Glycemic Control in Children with Recent-Onset Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus evaluates whether initiating an insulin pump or a continuous glucose monitor (CGM) within the first year of diagnosis is associated with reduced glycated hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c) levels in a cohort of 111 children aged 5 to 9 years with recent-onset type 1 diabetes. Tracking participants from baseline (mean diabetes duration of 4.7 months) to a 6-month follow-up (~12 months post-diagnosis), the study found that insulin pump usage grew from 17% to 35.1% and CGM usage increased from 17.1% to 25.2%. The findings demonstrate that children using an insulin pump maintained lower overall HbA1c levels compared to non-users, and children who started using a CGM during this timeframe experienced significantly lower HbA1c levels than those who did not. Based on these findings, the authors conclude and recommend that early initiation of either an insulin pump or a CGM in newly diagnosed children can help improve glycemic control within their first year of living with type 1 diabetes.

The study found that HIT-enhanced SMBG alone resulted in no change in mean HbA1c, family-centered goal setting showed a non-significant decrease of 0.3% at 6 months, and the combined approach demonstrated a significant HbA1c reduction of 0.6% at 3 months that diminished to a non-significant 0.4% reduction by 6 months, with higher baseline HbA1c levels predicting greater improvement; additionally, there were no significant changes or group differences in the daily frequency of SMBG testing. Based on these findings, the authors recommend further research into pairing family-centered goal setting with HIT-enhanced diabetes technologies, noting that family goal setting and counseling may be particularly useful when adolescents adopt new self-management technologies to achieve optimal clinical outcomes, especially among those with higher baseline HbA1c levels.

question: What major healthcare organizations recognize pediatric psychologists as essential members of the interdisciplinary diabetes care team?
passage_1: The paper, "Contemporary Roles of the Pediatric Psychologist in Diabetes Care," evaluates the diverse clinical, administrative, and research roles that pediatric psychologists play in managing diabetes among children and adolescents across various treatment phases—including diagnosis, outpatient visits, and inpatient hospitalizations—and settings such as academic medical centers, private practice, and community organizations. Findings highlight that major healthcare organizations recognize psychologists as essential members of the interdisciplinary diabetes care team, contributing through screening, individual, family, and group interventions, as well as translational research and program development for youth transitioning to adult care. The authors recommend embedding pediatric psychologists directly into integrated diabetes clinics to deliver comprehensive medical and psychosocial care in a single visit, alongside increasing advocacy to expand clinical engagement, billing models, and translational research opportunities in pediatric diabetes management.
passage_2: The Hvidoere Childhood Diabetes Study Group Centre Differences Study 2005 evaluates the glycaemic targets set by diabetes teams, how these targets are perceived by adolescents with type 1 diabetes and their parents, and their overall influence on metabolic control across 21 international centres. In an assessment of 2,062 adolescents, the study found a mean HbA1c of 8.2%, with significant variation between centres ranging from 7.4% to 9.1%. Key findings revealed a significant positive correlation between the HbA1c levels that adolescents and parents reported they would be happy with—as well as their perceived ideal targets—and their actual HbA1c results, with lower target HbA1c setting and greater consistency among multidisciplinary team members directly associating with lower overall centre HbA1c levels. Ultimately, the paper concludes that target setting plays a significant role in driving the metabolic differences observed across centres, demonstrating that clear and consistent setting of glycaemic targets by pediatric diabetes teams strongly improves HbA1c outcomes.
passage_3: Behavioral Diabetes: Social Ecological Perspectives for Pediatric and Adult Populations evaluates the complex interaction of psychosocial, behavioral, and ecological factors in managing diabetes across pediatric and adult age groups, emphasizing that optimal glycemic control relies heavily on addressing daily life stressors and psychological well-being alongside standard medical treatment. The text finds that psychosocial stressors significantly impact patient and family adherence to diabetes care routines, making behavioral support a critical component of effective disease management. To improve patient outcomes, it recommends integrating behaviorally oriented specialists into diabetes care teams and addressing the broader social and environmental contexts surrounding individuals with diabetes.

question: In the decision-making involvement study, which DMI behaviors were significantly associated with higher overall treatment adherence in both parent and youth reports?
passage_1: The study Decision-Making Involvement and Prediction of Adherence in Youth With Type 1 Diabetes: A Cohort Sequential Study evaluates developmental trajectories of decision-making involvement (DMI)—defined as the ways in which parents and children engage each other regarding T1D management—and examines how DMI impacts adherence levels and age-related changes over time in youth aged 8 to 16 assessed five times over two years. Findings revealed that most DMI aspects increased with age, though certain child-reported subscales (Parent Express, Child Seek, and Joint) peaked around ages 12–14 before declining; additionally, higher levels of Child Seek, Child Express, and Joint behaviors were significantly associated with higher overall treatment adherence in both parent and youth reports, though DMI did not significantly alter the rate of adherence decline over time. Recommendations and guidelines suggest targeting interventions toward encouraging proactive child participation in T1D discussions—specifically coaching youth to share information, express opinions, and solicit parental guidance—to support effective self-management as children transition toward greater autonomy.
passage_2: The study Youth Involvement in the Decision to Start CGM Predicts Subsequent CGM Use evaluates whether youth involvement in the decision to initiate continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) influences subsequent CGM adherence, and tests whether CGM self-efficacy and perceived hassle mediate this relationship among parent-youth dyads. The findings reveal that youth involvement in the initial decision positively predicted CGM use between weeks 5 and 12, mediated by the youth perceiving higher self-efficacy and lower hassle at a 2-month follow-up. Based on these findings, the authors recommend that healthcare providers actively facilitate youth participation and input when deciding to initiate CGM therapy in order to maximize long-term device adherence and clinical benefits.
passage_3: This study, titled Electronically Verified Use of Internet-Based, Multimedia Decision Aids by Adolescents With Type 1 Diabetes and Their Caregivers evaluates the actual, electronically tracked utilization of web-based decision aids by adolescents with type 1 diabetes and their caregivers considering an insulin pump or continuous glucose monitor within a randomized controlled trial. Findings indicate that 80% of caregivers and 66% of adolescents logged into a decision aid at least once, spending an average of 55.0 and 46.2 minutes on the website and viewing 72.2% and 77.4% of the content, respectively. Bivariate and regression analyses revealed that non-Hispanic, Caucasian females from higher socioeconomic status households were significantly more likely to log in, while adolescent males with lower health literacy demonstrated fewer logins. Based on these results, the paper recommends that future shared decision-making trials seek to actively promote decision aid engagement—particularly among non-White adolescents, potentially via direct assistance during the initial login—and explicitly guidelines that trials employing electronic decision aids routinely measure, report, and analyze objective utilization data.

question: In the study on disturbed eating behavior in Norwegian adolescents, what percentage reported restricting insulin and omitting insulin entirely after overeating?
passage_1: Disturbed Eating Behavior and Omission of Insulin in Adolescents Receiving Intensified Insulin Treatment evaluates the prevalence of disturbed eating behavior (DEB) and insulin restriction or omission among 770 Norwegian adolescents aged 11–19 with type 1 diabetes using the Diabetes Eating Problem Survey-Revised (DEPS-R). The findings indicate that 27.7% of females and 8.6% of males scored above the threshold for DEB, with prevalence increasing significantly alongside higher age and weight categories (reaching 38.1% in the oldest age group and 32.7% among obese participants). Additionally, 31.6% of participants reported restricting insulin and 6.9% reported omitting insulin entirely after overeating. Both DEB and insulin restriction were significantly associated with higher HbA1c levels (9.2% vs. 8.4% for DEB; 9.0% vs. 8.3% for restriction), highlighting poorer metabolic control and elevated risk for long-term diabetes complications. The paper emphasizes the need for early identification and further clinical assessment of at-risk individuals, as well as the importance of early intervention to prevent the development of full-threshold eating disorders and mitigate severe health risks.
passage_2: Disordered Eating Behaviors in Youth and Young Adults With Type 1 or Type 2 Diabetes Receiving Insulin Therapy:The SEARCH for Diabetes in Youth Study evaluates the prevalence of disordered eating behaviors (DEB) and their associations with glycemic control, insulin sensitivity, and psychosocial functioning in youth and young adults with type 1 or type 2 diabetes receiving insulin therapy. Analyzing a cohort of 2,156 participants with type 1 diabetes and 149 participants with type 2 diabetes using the Diabetes Eating Problem Survey–Revised (DEPS-R), the study found that DEB was present in 21.2% of individuals with type 1 diabetes and 50.3% of those with type 2 diabetes. Across both diabetes types, participants experiencing DEB demonstrated higher BMI z scores, lower insulin sensitivity, increased depressive symptoms, and a lower quality of life compared to those without DEB, with diabetic ketoacidosis episodes occurring significantly more often in type 1 diabetes participants with DEB. Based on these findings, the paper recommends heightened clinical awareness and early interventions tailored to address disordered eating in this vulnerable population, alongside calling for future longitudinal studies to track the long-term trajectory of DEB and its impact on diabetes outcomes.
passage_3: The systematic review Screening and identification of disordered eating in people with type 1 diabetes: A systematic review evaluates the reliability, validity, and clinical utility of 48 individual tools used to screen or identify disordered eating behaviors and eating disorders in individuals with Type 1 Diabetes across 90 studies. The authors found that the overall quality of the reported tools was poor, with a high risk of bias stemming from the widespread use of non-validated assessment tools and a lack of comparison against the reference standard of a diagnostic clinical interview. While the review notes that current guidelines suggest routine screening for disordered eating in people with Type 1 Diabetes due to elevated risk and associated health complications, it highlights a critical lack of evidence regarding which specific tools are most valid and reliable across different age groups and clinical settings. Consequently, the authors recommend that future research focus on evaluating the validity and reliability of available screening tools by directly comparing them against gold-standard diagnostic interviews to help establish standardized screening guidelines and improve clinical outcomes.

The study found that HIT-enhanced SMBG alone resulted in no change in mean HbA1c, family-centered goal setting showed a non-significant decrease of 0.3% at 6 months, and the combined approach demonstrated a significant HbA1c reduction of 0.6% at 3 months that diminished to a non-significant 0.4% reduction by 6 months, with higher baseline HbA1c levels predicting greater improvement; additionally, there were no significant changes or group differences in the daily frequency of SMBG testing. Based on these findings, the authors recommend further research into pairing family-centered goal setting with HIT-enhanced diabetes technologies, noting that family goal setting and counseling may be particularly useful when adolescents adopt new self-management technologies to achieve optimal clinical outcomes, especially among those with higher baseline HbA1c levels.
passage_2: Family-based Psychoeducation and Care Ambassador Intervention to Improve Glycemic Control in Youth with Type 1 Diabetes: A Randomized Trial evaluates the impact of a 2-year randomized clinical trial testing three levels of care—standard care with basic care coordination, monthly outreach by a Care Ambassador (CA), and monthly CA outreach plus quarterly family-based psychoeducation—on glycemic control (A1C), parental involvement, family conflict, and quality of life among 153 youth with type 1 diabetes. The findings revealed no overall significant differences in A1C across the three groups at the end of two years, and monthly outreach alone provided no added benefit over standard care when regular quarterly clinic visits were maintained; however, a subgroup analysis of youth with suboptimal baseline control (A1C ≥ 8%) showed that the psychoeducational intervention significantly helped maintain or improve A1C levels (77% vs. 52%) and sustain parent involvement (36% vs. 11%) compared to the combined non-psychoeducation groups, all without increasing diabetes-specific family conflict or decreasing youth quality of life. Based on these findings, the authors implicitly recommend incorporating structured psychoeducational strategies—focused on teamwork, setting realistic expectations, and joint problem-solving—alongside routine care coordination specifically for youth with suboptimal glycemic control, while cautioning against relying solely on frequent phone or email outreach without targeted behavioral support
passage_3: Effect of Continuous Glucose Monitoring on Glycemic Control in Adolescents and Young Adults With Type 1 Diabetes: A Randomized Clinical Trial evaluates the impact of continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) compared with standard blood glucose monitoring (BGM) on glycemic control over 26 weeks in 153 adolescents and young adults aged 14 to 24 years with type 1 diabetes. The study found that treatment with CGM resulted in a statistically significant reduction in mean HbA1c levels from 8.9% at baseline to 8.5% at 26 weeks, compared to remaining unchanged at 8.9% in the BGM group (an adjusted between-group difference of -0.37%). Additionally, participants in the CGM group demonstrated improvements in secondary outcomes, including time spent in the target glucose range and reduced daytime and nighttime glucose variability. The study concludes that CGM leads to small but statistically significant improvements in glycemic control in this population and notes that further research is needed to determine the clinical importance and long-term implications of these findings.

passage_1: The paper, "Contemporary Roles of the Pediatric Psychologist in Diabetes Care," evaluates the diverse clinical, administrative, and research roles that pediatric psychologists play in managing diabetes among children and adolescents across various treatment phases—including diagnosis, outpatient visits, and inpatient hospitalizations—and settings such as academic medical centers, private practice, and community organizations. Findings highlight that major healthcare organizations recognize psychologists as essential members of the interdisciplinary diabetes care team, contributing through screening, individual, family, and group interventions, as well as translational research and program development for youth transitioning to adult care. The authors recommend embedding pediatric psychologists directly into integrated diabetes clinics to deliver comprehensive medical and psychosocial care in a single visit, alongside increasing advocacy to expand clinical engagement, billing models, and translational research opportunities in pediatric diabetes management.
passage_2: The study titled Type 1 Diabetes Through the Life Span: A Position Statement of the American Diabetes Association evaluates the global and domestic incidence, diagnostic challenges, and comprehensive management strategies for type 1 diabetes across all age groups. It finds that type 1 diabetes is characterized by autoimmune beta-cell destruction leading to lifelong insulin dependence, affecting millions globally with substantial age-related and geographic variation in incidence. The study recommends recognizing clinical presentation variations between youth and adults, utilizing pancreatic autoantibody panels to differentiate type 1 from type 2 diabetes, and establishing early, structured transition plans from pediatric to adult clinical care teams. Additionally, guidelines provided in the paper outline standardized diagnostic criteria—such as fasting plasma glucose and A1C thresholds—alongside scheduled protocols for initial, quarterly, and annual evaluations covering microvascular and macrovascular complication screenings, autoimmune comorbidity checks, and individualized self-management support across all developmental stages.
passage_3: Longitudinal Trends in Glycemic Outcomes and Technology Use for Over 48,000 People with Type 1 Diabetes (2016–2022) from the T1D Exchange Quality Improvement Collaborative evaluates longitudinal trends in glycemic control (HbA1c) and diabetes technology adoption across more than 48,000 individuals with type 1 diabetes, stratified by race/ethnicity and insurance status. The findings show an overall clinically significant improvement in average HbA1c levels from 8.7% in 2016–2017 to 8.4% in 2021–2022, accompanied by a rise in participants reaching target HbA1c levels (<7%) from 20% to 26% and a decrease in those with severe hyperglycemia (>9%) from 43% to 31%. Alongside these glycemic gains, the uptake of diabetes technology increased significantly across continuous glucose monitors, insulin pumps, and hybrid closed-loop systems; however, pronounced health inequities persisted, as non-Hispanic White and privately insured individuals consistently maintained better glycemic outcomes and higher device adoption rates than non-Hispanic Black, Hispanic, and publicly insured patients. Based on these insights, the study highlights the need for targeted quality improvement interventions, policy adjustments, and funded research to directly address socio-behavioral barriers and ensure equitable access to diabetes technology and care across diverse populations.

passage_1: The study Decision-Making Involvement and Prediction of Adherence in Youth With Type 1 Diabetes: A Cohort Sequential Study evaluates developmental trajectories of decision-making involvement (DMI)—defined as the ways in which parents and children engage each other regarding T1D management—and examines how DMI impacts adherence levels and age-related changes over time in youth aged 8 to 16 assessed five times over two years. Findings revealed that most DMI aspects increased with age, though certain child-reported subscales (Parent Express, Child Seek, and Joint) peaked around ages 12–14 before declining; additionally, higher levels of Child Seek, Child Express, and Joint behaviors were significantly associated with higher overall treatment adherence in both parent and youth reports, though DMI did not significantly alter the rate of adherence decline over time. Recommendations and guidelines suggest targeting interventions toward encouraging proactive child participation in T1D discussions—specifically coaching youth to share information, express opinions, and solicit parental guidance—to support effective self-management as children transition toward greater autonomy.
passage_2: This study, titled Electronically Verified Use of Internet-Based, Multimedia Decision Aids by Adolescents With Type 1 Diabetes and Their Caregivers evaluates the actual, electronically tracked utilization of web-based decision aids by adolescents with type 1 diabetes and their caregivers considering an insulin pump or continuous glucose monitor within a randomized controlled trial. Findings indicate that 80% of caregivers and 66% of adolescents logged into a decision aid at least once, spending an average of 55.0 and 46.2 minutes on the website and viewing 72.2% and 77.4% of the content, respectively. Bivariate and regression analyses revealed that non-Hispanic, Caucasian females from higher socioeconomic status households were significantly more likely to log in, while adolescent males with lower health literacy demonstrated fewer logins. Based on these results, the paper recommends that future shared decision-making trials seek to actively promote decision aid engagement—particularly among non-White adolescents, potentially via direct assistance during the initial login—and explicitly guidelines that trials employing electronic decision aids routinely measure, report, and analyze objective utilization data.
passage_3: The SWEET Project 10-Year Benchmarking study evaluates time trends of key quality indicators and the impact of treatment changes in 16,082 youth with type 1 diabetes across 22 centers in 19 countries between 2008–2010 and 2016–2018. Over the 10-year period, adjusted mean HbA1c significantly improved from 68 mmol/mol (8.4%) to 63 mmol/mol (7.9%), coinciding with an increase in insulin pump use from 25.7% to 41.8% and continuous glucose monitoring sensor use from 1.5% to 44.6%. The percentage of patients achieving the target HbA1c of <7% (<53 mmol/mol) rose from 21% in 2008 to 34% in 2018, while severe hypoglycemia rates dropped from 3.8% to 2.4%, and secondary cardiovascular risk factors such as BMI-standard deviation score improved. The findings suggest that twice-yearly international benchmarking, standardized quality control, continuous data monitoring, and the adoption of modern diabetes technologies within centers of reference are effective strategies for improving long-term metabolic outcomes in pediatric type 1 diabetes care.

The study found that median HbA1c peaked in late adolescence at 9.3% for females at age 17 and 9.1% for males at age 19, with overall target HbA1c levels achieved by very few participants (only 11% of adolescents aged 14–17 and 7% of young adults aged 18–25). Microvascular complications were prevalent, with 16% of participants exhibiting retinopathy and 13% exhibiting nephropathy; higher HbA1c levels across adolescence and young adulthood, longer diabetes duration, younger age at diagnosis, and smoking were strongly associated with a higher risk of complications. Additionally, patients who transferred to adult care before age 18 had significantly higher HbA1c levels and a higher prevalence of complications than those who transferred between ages 18–22, while less than 40% of patients with albuminuria were receiving recommended ACE inhibitor or ARB treatment. Based on these findings, the paper recommends that pediatricians and endocrinologists critically assess the care offered to adolescents and young adults, adopt new approaches to help improve glycemic control during the vulnerable late-teen years, optimize transition strategies to adult care, and strictly adhere to clinical guidelines regarding blood pressure and kidney protection medications for patients with nephropathy.

The study found that the relative risk for severe hypoglycemia and coma per 1% HbA1c decrease declined significantly from 1.28 to 1.05 and from 1.39 to 1.01, respectively, over the 18-year period, alongside a continuous increase in daily blood glucose monitoring frequency, short- and long-acting insulin analog use, and continuous subcutaneous insulin infusion pump therapy. Based on these findings, the paper indicates that lower HbA1c levels have become a minor predictor for severe hypoglycemia, allowing clinicians and young patients with type 1 diabetes to aim for near-normal glycemic control to prevent long-term diabetic complications without substantially increasing their risk of severe hypoglycemic events.

passage_1: Hemoglobin A1c measurement for the diagnosis of Type 2 diabetes in children evaluates the utility, reliability, and methodology of using laboratory-based HbA1c testing for diagnosing Type 2 diabetes in pediatric populations, addressing recent studies that dismissed HbA1c due to poor correlation with Oral Glucose Tolerance Tests (OGTT) or Fasting Plasma Glucose (FPG). The authors find that rejecting HbA1c based on lack of correlation with OGTT or FPG is scientifically flawed because neither OGTT nor FPG have themselves been validated against long-term health outcomes (such as retinopathy) in children, and OGTT suffers from low reproducibility. Additionally, non-fasting HbA1c screening is more practical, reproducible, and has been shown to increase diabetes screening rates and early detection among adolescents. The paper recommends that American Diabetes Association (ADA) diagnostic criteria remain useful for screening at-risk, asymptomatic or minimally symptomatic pediatric populations, with laboratory-based HbA1c certified by the National Glycohemoglobin Standardization Program (NGSP) being the preferred method; practitioners should exercise clinical judgment when diagnostic test results conflict, and HbA1c should be avoided in cases of pregnancy, cystic fibrosis, or hemoglobinopathies and disorders causing high red blood cell turnover.

It finds that type 1 diabetes is characterized by autoimmune beta-cell destruction leading to lifelong insulin dependence, affecting millions globally with substantial age-related and geographic variation in incidence. The study recommends recognizing clinical presentation variations between youth and adults, utilizing pancreatic autoantibody panels to differentiate type 1 from type 2 diabetes, and establishing early, structured transition plans from pediatric to adult clinical care teams. Additionally, guidelines provided in the paper outline standardized diagnostic criteria—such as fasting plasma glucose and A1C thresholds—alongside scheduled protocols for initial, quarterly, and annual evaluations covering microvascular and macrovascular complication screenings, autoimmune comorbidity checks, and individualized self-management support across all developmental stages.

Confirmed undiagnosed diabetes was rare (less than 0.5% of youth), with over 85% of diabetes cases already diagnosed. Furthermore, HbA1c-defined hyperglycemia showed significantly stronger and more specific associations with cardiometabolic risk compared to FPG-defined hyperglycemia. Based on these findings, the study highlights HbA1c as a highly specific, effective nonfasting test to identify high-risk youth who could benefit from lifestyle interventions to prevent diabetes and cardiovascular risks later in life.

The findings reveal that youth involvement in the initial decision positively predicted CGM use between weeks 5 and 12, mediated by the youth perceiving higher self-efficacy and lower hassle at a 2-month follow-up. Based on these findings, the authors recommend that healthcare providers actively facilitate youth participation and input when deciding to initiate CGM therapy in order to maximize long-term device adherence and clinical benefits.

The study found that treatment with CGM resulted in a statistically significant reduction in mean HbA1c levels from 8.9% at baseline to 8.5% at 26 weeks, compared to remaining unchanged at 8.9% in the BGM group (an adjusted between-group difference of -0.37%). Additionally, participants in the CGM group demonstrated improvements in secondary outcomes, including time spent in the target glucose range and reduced daytime and nighttime glucose variability. The study concludes that CGM leads to small but statistically significant improvements in glycemic control in this population and notes that further research is needed to determine the clinical importance and long-term implications of these findings.

question: Does the Norwegian disturbed eating behavior study provide data on the effectiveness of specific eating disorder treatments in reducing insulin omission and improving HbA1c?
passage_1: Disturbed Eating Behavior and Omission of Insulin in Adolescents Receiving Intensified Insulin Treatment evaluates the prevalence of disturbed eating behavior (DEB) and insulin restriction or omission among 770 Norwegian adolescents aged 11–19 with type 1 diabetes using the Diabetes Eating Problem Survey-Revised (DEPS-R). The findings indicate that 27.7% of females and 8.6% of males scored above the threshold for DEB, with prevalence increasing significantly alongside higher age and weight categories (reaching 38.1% in the oldest age group and 32.7% among obese participants). Additionally, 31.6% of participants reported restricting insulin and 6.9% reported omitting insulin entirely after overeating. Both DEB and insulin restriction were significantly associated with higher HbA1c levels (9.2% vs. 8.4% for DEB; 9.0% vs. 8.3% for restriction), highlighting poorer metabolic control and elevated risk for long-term diabetes complications. The paper emphasizes the need for early identification and further clinical assessment of at-risk individuals, as well as the importance of early intervention to prevent the development of full-threshold eating disorders and mitigate severe health risks.
passage_2: The systematic review Screening and identification of disordered eating in people with type 1 diabetes: A systematic review evaluates the reliability, validity, and clinical utility of 48 individual tools used to screen or identify disordered eating behaviors and eating disorders in individuals with Type 1 Diabetes across 90 studies. The authors found that the overall quality of the reported tools was poor, with a high risk of bias stemming from the widespread use of non-validated assessment tools and a lack of comparison against the reference standard of a diagnostic clinical interview. While the review notes that current guidelines suggest routine screening for disordered eating in people with Type 1 Diabetes due to elevated risk and associated health complications, it highlights a critical lack of evidence regarding which specific tools are most valid and reliable across different age groups and clinical settings. Consequently, the authors recommend that future research focus on evaluating the validity and reliability of available screening tools by directly comparing them against gold-standard diagnostic interviews to help establish standardized screening guidelines and improve clinical outcomes.

In an assessment of 2,062 adolescents, the study found a mean HbA1c of 8.2%, with significant variation between centres ranging from 7.4% to 9.1%. Key findings revealed a significant positive correlation between the HbA1c levels that adolescents and parents reported they would be happy with—as well as their perceived ideal targets—and their actual HbA1c results, with lower target HbA1c setting and greater consistency among multidisciplinary team members directly associating with lower overall centre HbA1c levels. Ultimately, the paper concludes that target setting plays a significant role in driving the metabolic differences observed across centres, demonstrating that clear and consistent setting of glycaemic targets by pediatric diabetes teams strongly improves HbA1c outcomes.

question: What are the specific patient-level factors (beyond HbA1c) that predict which youth will benefit most from early insulin pump versus early CGM initiation in the recent-onset study?
passage_1: Early Initiation of Diabetes Devices Relates to Improved Glycemic Control in Children with Recent-Onset Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus evaluates whether initiating an insulin pump or a continuous glucose monitor (CGM) within the first year of diagnosis is associated with reduced glycated hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c) levels in a cohort of 111 children aged 5 to 9 years with recent-onset type 1 diabetes. Tracking participants from baseline (mean diabetes duration of 4.7 months) to a 6-month follow-up (~12 months post-diagnosis), the study found that insulin pump usage grew from 17% to 35.1% and CGM usage increased from 17.1% to 25.2%. The findings demonstrate that children using an insulin pump maintained lower overall HbA1c levels compared to non-users, and children who started using a CGM during this timeframe experienced significantly lower HbA1c levels than those who did not. Based on these findings, the authors conclude and recommend that early initiation of either an insulin pump or a CGM in newly diagnosed children can help improve glycemic control within their first year of living with type 1 diabetes.
passage_2: The SWEET Project 10-Year Benchmarking study evaluates time trends of key quality indicators and the impact of treatment changes in 16,082 youth with type 1 diabetes across 22 centers in 19 countries between 2008–2010 and 2016–2018. Over the 10-year period, adjusted mean HbA1c significantly improved from 68 mmol/mol (8.4%) to 63 mmol/mol (7.9%), coinciding with an increase in insulin pump use from 25.7% to 41.8% and continuous glucose monitoring sensor use from 1.5% to 44.6%. The percentage of patients achieving the target HbA1c of <7% (<53 mmol/mol) rose from 21% in 2008 to 34% in 2018, while severe hypoglycemia rates dropped from 3.8% to 2.4%, and secondary cardiovascular risk factors such as BMI-standard deviation score improved. The findings suggest that twice-yearly international benchmarking, standardized quality control, continuous data monitoring, and the adoption of modern diabetes technologies within centers of reference are effective strategies for improving long-term metabolic outcomes in pediatric type 1 diabetes care.
passage_3: The study Hemoglobin A1c Levels and Risk of Severe Hypoglycemia in Children and Young Adults with Type 1 Diabetes from Germany and Austria: A Trend Analysis in a Cohort of 37,539 Patients between 1995 and 2012 evaluates temporal trends in the association between hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c) levels and the risk of severe hypoglycemia or hypoglycemic coma in a prospective cohort of 37,539 children and young adults with type 1 diabetes from Germany and Austria between 1995 and 2012. The study found that the relative risk for severe hypoglycemia and coma per 1% HbA1c decrease declined significantly from 1.28 to 1.05 and from 1.39 to 1.01, respectively, over the 18-year period, alongside a continuous increase in daily blood glucose monitoring frequency, short- and long-acting insulin analog use, and continuous subcutaneous insulin infusion pump therapy. Based on these findings, the paper indicates that lower HbA1c levels have become a minor predictor for severe hypoglycemia, allowing clinicians and young patients with type 1 diabetes to aim for near-normal glycemic control to prevent long-term diabetic complications without substantially increasing their risk of severe hypoglycemic events.

question: What carbohydrate ingestion enhances high-intensity running capacity according to the acute effects of carbohydrate supplementation on intermittent sports performance study?
passage_1: Acute effects of carbohydrate supplementation on intermittent sports performance evaluates the biological mechanisms and performance outcomes of consuming carbohydrates during intermittent high-intensity team sports lasting roughly 1 to 2 hours. Drawing on energy system demands that rely heavily on muscle glycogen and blood glucose, the review finds that carbohydrate ingestion generally enhances high-intensity running capacity, delays fatigue, and helps maintain sport-specific technical skills towards the end of prolonged play. Based on these findings, the paper recommends carbohydrate intake during prolonged intermittent exertion to preserve plasma glucose oxidation and central nervous system function, providing guidelines that favor consuming 30 to 60 grams of carbohydrate per hour—or utilizing carbohydrate mouth rinsing for shorter high-intensity sessions—to optimize overall athletic performance.
passage_2: Personalized Approach for the Management of Exercise-Related Glycemic Imbalances in Type 1 Diabetes: Comparison with Reference Method evaluates the efficacy of the personalized Exercise Carbohydrate Requirement Estimation System (ECRES) algorithm against a reference tabular approach to estimate extra carbohydrate requirements for preventing exercise-induced hypoglycemia in 26 adults with type 1 diabetes. The study found that the ECRES algorithm calculated a significantly lower median carbohydrate intake overall compared to the tabular approach (13.5 g vs. 23.0 g; P < .01), which was particularly marked in physically active participants (9.0 g vs. 23.0 g; P < .01), while both methods successfully prevented hypoglycemia during exercise; post-exercise, ECRES maintained continuous glucose monitoring metrics within recommended target guidelines, whereas the tabular method resulted in significantly higher time below range in the afternoon (11.8% vs. target <4%; P < .05) and time above range during the night (39.3% vs. target <25%; P < .05).
passage_3: Hemoglobin A1c measurement for the diagnosis of Type 2 diabetes in children evaluates the utility, reliability, and methodology of using laboratory-based HbA1c testing for diagnosing Type 2 diabetes in pediatric populations, addressing recent studies that dismissed HbA1c due to poor correlation with Oral Glucose Tolerance Tests (OGTT) or Fasting Plasma Glucose (FPG). The authors find that rejecting HbA1c based on lack of correlation with OGTT or FPG is scientifically flawed because neither OGTT nor FPG have themselves been validated against long-term health outcomes (such as retinopathy) in children, and OGTT suffers from low reproducibility. Additionally, non-fasting HbA1c screening is more practical, reproducible, and has been shown to increase diabetes screening rates and early detection among adolescents. The paper recommends that American Diabetes Association (ADA) diagnostic criteria remain useful for screening at-risk, asymptomatic or minimally symptomatic pediatric populations, with laboratory-based HbA1c certified by the National Glycohemoglobin Standardization Program (NGSP) being the preferred method; practitioners should exercise clinical judgment when diagnostic test results conflict, and HbA1c should be avoided in cases of pregnancy, cystic fibrosis, or hemoglobinopathies and disorders causing high red blood cell turnover.

question: According to the advancing diabetes management in adolescents: comparative effectiveness of mobil research, three arms: HIT-enhanced meter, family-centered goal setting, combined?

The study found that HIT-enhanced SMBG alone resulted in no change in mean HbA1c, family-centered goal setting showed a non-significant decrease of 0.3% at 6 months, and the combined approach demonstrated a significant HbA1c reduction of 0.6% at 3 months that diminished to a non-significant 0.4% reduction by 6 months, with higher baseline HbA1c levels predicting greater improvement; additionally, there were no significant changes or group differences in the daily frequency of SMBG testing. Based on these findings, the authors recommend further research into pairing family-centered goal setting with HIT-enhanced diabetes technologies, noting that family goal setting and counseling may be particularly useful when adolescents adopt new self-management technologies to achieve optimal clinical outcomes, especially among those with higher baseline HbA1c levels.
passage_2: Family-based Psychoeducation and Care Ambassador Intervention to Improve Glycemic Control in Youth with Type 1 Diabetes: A Randomized Trial evaluates the impact of a 2-year randomized clinical trial testing three levels of care—standard care with basic care coordination, monthly outreach by a Care Ambassador (CA), and monthly CA outreach plus quarterly family-based psychoeducation—on glycemic control (A1C), parental involvement, family conflict, and quality of life among 153 youth with type 1 diabetes. Based on these findings, the authors implicitly recommend incorporating structured psychoeducational strategies—focused on teamwork, setting realistic expectations, and joint problem-solving—alongside routine care coordination specifically for youth with suboptimal glycemic control, while cautioning against relying solely on frequent phone or email outreach without targeted behavioral support

In an assessment of 2,062 adolescents, the study found a mean HbA1c of 8.2%, with significant variation between centres ranging from 7.4% to 9.1%. Key findings revealed a significant positive correlation between the HbA1c levels that adolescents and parents reported they would be happy with—as well as their perceived ideal targets—and their actual HbA1c results, with lower target HbA1c setting and greater consistency among multidisciplinary team members directly associating with lower overall centre HbA1c levels. question: According to the contemporary roles of pediatric psychologist in diabetes care research, roles span diagnosis, outpatient visits, inpatient hospitalizations?

Findings highlight that major healthcare organizations recognize psychologists as essential members of the interdisciplinary diabetes care team, contributing through screening, individual, family, and group interventions, as well as translational research and program development for youth transitioning to adult care. The authors recommend embedding pediatric psychologists directly into integrated diabetes clinics to deliver comprehensive medical and psychosocial care in a single visit, alongside increasing advocacy to expand clinical engagement, billing models, and translational research opportunities in pediatric diabetes management.

passage_1: The study Decision-Making Involvement and Prediction of Adherence in Youth With Type 1 Diabetes: A Cohort Sequential Study evaluates developmental trajectories of decision-making involvement (DMI)—defined as the ways in which parents and children engage each other regarding T1D management—and examines how DMI impacts adherence levels and age-related changes over time in youth aged 8 to 16 assessed five times over two years. Findings revealed that most DMI aspects increased with age, though certain child-reported subscales (Parent Express, Child Seek, and Joint) peaked around ages 12–14 before declining; additionally, higher levels of Child Seek, Child Express, and Joint behaviors were significantly associated with higher overall treatment adherence in both parent and youth reports, though DMI did not significantly alter the rate of adherence decline over time. Recommendations and guidelines suggest targeting interventions toward encouraging proactive child participation in T1D discussions—specifically coaching youth to share information, express opinions, and solicit parental guidance—to support effective self-management as children transition toward greater autonomy.

question: According to the disordered eating behaviors and eating disorders in youth with type 2 diabetes research, approximately half had elevated scores on Diabetes Eating Problem Survey-Revised?
passage_1: "Disordered Eating Behaviors and Eating Disorders in Youth With Type 2 Diabetes: A Systematic Review" evaluates disordered eating behaviors (DEBs) in youth diagnosed with type 2 diabetes by identifying the most common DEBs, analyzing potential risk and protective factors, and reviewing existing screening tools and interventions utilized for this population. Findings indicate that approximately half of the youth study participants had elevated scores on the Diabetes Eating Problem Survey–Revised, showing a higher likelihood of engaging in DEBs compared to youth with type 1 diabetes, with key risk factors including obesity, body weight/shape concerns, and caregiver subclinical binge eating. Recommendations highlight a critical need for further research to construct a framework for understanding influential variables, to advance screening tools, and to design effective targeted interventions.
passage_2: Disordered Eating Behaviors in Youth and Young Adults With Type 1 or Type 2 Diabetes Receiving Insulin Therapy:The SEARCH for Diabetes in Youth Study evaluates the prevalence of disordered eating behaviors (DEB) and their associations with glycemic control, insulin sensitivity, and psychosocial functioning in youth and young adults with type 1 or type 2 diabetes receiving insulin therapy. Analyzing a cohort of 2,156 participants with type 1 diabetes and 149 participants with type 2 diabetes using the Diabetes Eating Problem Survey–Revised (DEPS-R), the study found that DEB was present in 21.2% of individuals with type 1 diabetes and 50.3% of those with type 2 diabetes. Across both diabetes types, participants experiencing DEB demonstrated higher BMI z scores, lower insulin sensitivity, increased depressive symptoms, and a lower quality of life compared to those without DEB, with diabetic ketoacidosis episodes occurring significantly more often in type 1 diabetes participants with DEB. Based on these findings, the paper recommends heightened clinical awareness and early interventions tailored to address disordered eating in this vulnerable population, alongside calling for future longitudinal studies to track the long-term trajectory of DEB and its impact on diabetes outcomes.

The findings indicate that 27.7% of females and 8.6% of males scored above the threshold for DEB, with prevalence increasing significantly alongside higher age and weight categories (reaching 38.1% in the oldest age group and 32.7% among obese participants). Additionally, 31.6% of participants reported restricting insulin and 6.9% reported omitting insulin entirely after overeating. Both DEB and insulin restriction were significantly associated with higher HbA1c levels (9.2% vs. 8.4% for DEB; 9.0% vs. 8.3% for restriction), highlighting poorer metabolic control and elevated risk for long-term diabetes complications. The paper emphasizes the need for early identification and further clinical assessment of at-risk individuals, as well as the importance of early intervention to prevent the development of full-threshold eating disorders and mitigate severe health risks.

question: What CGM usage: 17.1% to 25.2% over follow-up according to the early initiation of diabetes devices relates to improved glycemic control in chi study?
passage_1: Early Initiation of Diabetes Devices Relates to Improved Glycemic Control in Children with Recent-Onset Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus evaluates whether initiating an insulin pump or a continuous glucose monitor (CGM) within the first year of diagnosis is associated with reduced glycated hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c) levels in a cohort of 111 children aged 5 to 9 years with recent-onset type 1 diabetes. Tracking participants from baseline (mean diabetes duration of 4.7 months) to a 6-month follow-up (~12 months post-diagnosis), the study found that insulin pump usage grew from 17% to 35.1% and CGM usage increased from 17.1% to 25.2%. The findings demonstrate that children using an insulin pump maintained lower overall HbA1c levels compared to non-users, and children who started using a CGM during this timeframe experienced significantly lower HbA1c levels than those who did not. Based on these findings, the authors conclude and recommend that early initiation of either an insulin pump or a CGM in newly diagnosed children can help improve glycemic control within their first year of living with type 1 diabetes.
passage_2: Effect of Continuous Glucose Monitoring on Glycemic Control in Adolescents and Young Adults With Type 1 Diabetes: A Randomized Clinical Trial evaluates the impact of continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) compared with standard blood glucose monitoring (BGM) on glycemic control over 26 weeks in 153 adolescents and young adults aged 14 to 24 years with type 1 diabetes. The study found that treatment with CGM resulted in a statistically significant reduction in mean HbA1c levels from 8.9% at baseline to 8.5% at 26 weeks, compared to remaining unchanged at 8.9% in the BGM group (an adjusted between-group difference of -0.37%). Additionally, participants in the CGM group demonstrated improvements in secondary outcomes, including time spent in the target glucose range and reduced daytime and nighttime glucose variability. The study concludes that CGM leads to small but statistically significant improvements in glycemic control in this population and notes that further research is needed to determine the clinical importance and long-term implications of these findings.
