The findings reveal that youth involvement in the initial decision positively predicted CGM use between weeks 5 and 12, mediated by the youth perceiving higher self-efficacy and lower hassle at a 2-month follow-up. Based on these findings, the authors recommend that healthcare providers actively facilitate youth participation and input when deciding to initiate CGM therapy in order to maximize long-term device adherence and clinical benefits.

passage_1: Family-based Psychoeducation and Care Ambassador Intervention to Improve Glycemic Control in Youth with Type 1 Diabetes: A Randomized Trial evaluates the impact of a 2-year randomized clinical trial testing three levels of care—standard care with basic care coordination, monthly outreach by a Care Ambassador (CA), and monthly CA outreach plus quarterly family-based psychoeducation—on glycemic control (A1C), parental involvement, family conflict, and quality of life among 153 youth with type 1 diabetes. The findings revealed no overall significant differences in A1C across the three groups at the end of two years, and monthly outreach alone provided no added benefit over standard care when regular quarterly clinic visits were maintained; however, a subgroup analysis of youth with suboptimal baseline control (A1C ≥ 8%) showed that the psychoeducational intervention significantly helped maintain or improve A1C levels (77% vs. 52%) and sustain parent involvement (36% vs. 11%) compared to the combined non-psychoeducation groups, all without increasing diabetes-specific family conflict or decreasing youth quality of life. Based on these findings, the authors implicitly recommend incorporating structured psychoeducational strategies—focused on teamwork, setting realistic expectations, and joint problem-solving—alongside routine care coordination specifically for youth with suboptimal glycemic control, while cautioning against relying solely on frequent phone or email outreach without targeted behavioral support

question: According to the personalized approach for management of exercise-related glycemic imbalances in research, ECRES algorithm vs reference tabular approach for exercise carb requirements?
passage_1: Personalized Approach for the Management of Exercise-Related Glycemic Imbalances in Type 1 Diabetes: Comparison with Reference Method evaluates the efficacy of the personalized Exercise Carbohydrate Requirement Estimation System (ECRES) algorithm against a reference tabular approach to estimate extra carbohydrate requirements for preventing exercise-induced hypoglycemia in 26 adults with type 1 diabetes. The study found that the ECRES algorithm calculated a significantly lower median carbohydrate intake overall compared to the tabular approach (13.5 g vs. 23.0 g; P < .01), which was particularly marked in physically active participants (9.0 g vs. 23.0 g; P < .01), while both methods successfully prevented hypoglycemia during exercise; post-exercise, ECRES maintained continuous glucose monitoring metrics within recommended target guidelines, whereas the tabular method resulted in significantly higher time below range in the afternoon (11.8% vs. target <4%; P < .05) and time above range during the night (39.3% vs. target <25%; P < .05).

Drawing on energy system demands that rely heavily on muscle glycogen and blood glucose, the review finds that carbohydrate ingestion generally enhances high-intensity running capacity, delays fatigue, and helps maintain sport-specific technical skills towards the end of prolonged play. Based on these findings, the paper recommends carbohydrate intake during prolonged intermittent exertion to preserve plasma glucose oxidation and central nervous system function, providing guidelines that favor consuming 30 to 60 grams of carbohydrate per hour—or utilizing carbohydrate mouth rinsing for shorter high-intensity sessions—to optimize overall athletic performance.

The study found that while 25.5% of US youth met screening criteria, the sensitivity and specificity of these criteria were low for detecting hyperglycemia. Confirmed undiagnosed diabetes was rare (less than 0.5% of youth), with over 85% of diabetes cases already diagnosed. Furthermore, HbA1c-defined hyperglycemia showed significantly stronger and more specific associations with cardiometabolic risk compared to FPG-defined hyperglycemia. The review found a 22.2% prevalence of depression and a 17.7% prevalence of anxiety among children with type 1 diabetes, with depression being notably higher in girls (29.7%) compared to boys (19.7%) and in lower-middle-income countries (29.3%), while the prevalence of depression among children with type 2 diabetes stood at 22.7%. Based on these findings, the study highlights the necessity of implementing extensive, periodic psychological screening and targeted interventions to identify and reduce pediatric depression in this vulnerable population.
passage_2: The study "Systematic Review: Diabetes Family Conflict in Young People With Type 1 Diabetes" evaluates the relationships between diabetes-specific family conflict and various health outcomes—including glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c), treatment adherence, blood glucose monitoring, depression, anxiety, quality of life, and well-being—among young people with type 1 diabetes aged 14 to 25 years. Across 20 included studies, greater diabetes-specific family conflict was significantly associated with higher HbA1c values in 17 studies, suboptimal treatment adherence or less frequent blood glucose monitoring in 7 studies, and poorer quality of life, reduced well-being, or heightened depressive and anxiety symptoms in 7 studies, though 4 studies found no significant links to HbA1c or adherence. Given these findings, the authors recommend routine screening for and intervention addressing diabetes-specific family conflict in clinical practice, while highlighting guidelines for future research to prioritize longitudinal studies specifically targeting young people over the age of 16.
passage_3: The TODAY2 study evaluates the prevalence and associated factors of high diabetes distress among young adults with youth-onset type 2 diabetes. Analyzing 438 participants, the researchers found that 24% reported high overall diabetes distress, with 40% experiencing high regimen distress and 29.7% experiencing high emotional burden. High distress was significantly associated with female sex, higher HbA1c levels, moderate-to-severe anxiety symptoms, and a lack of healthcare coverage, while moderate-to-severe depressive symptoms were linked to both regimen distress and emotional burden, and insulin treatment was specifically linked to emotional burden. The paper recommends that future research focus on identifying modifiable factors associated with high diabetes distress in order to inform targeted psychosocial interventions for this medically vulnerable group.

Confirmed undiagnosed diabetes was rare (less than 0.5% of youth), with over 85% of diabetes cases already diagnosed. Furthermore, HbA1c-defined hyperglycemia showed significantly stronger and more specific associations with cardiometabolic risk compared to FPG-defined hyperglycemia. question: According to the screening and identification of disordered eating in people with type 1 diabetes research, overall quality of tools: poor, high risk of bias?
passage_1: The systematic review Screening and identification of disordered eating in people with type 1 diabetes: A systematic review evaluates the reliability, validity, and clinical utility of 48 individual tools used to screen or identify disordered eating behaviors and eating disorders in individuals with Type 1 Diabetes across 90 studies. The authors found that the overall quality of the reported tools was poor, with a high risk of bias stemming from the widespread use of non-validated assessment tools and a lack of comparison against the reference standard of a diagnostic clinical interview. While the review notes that current guidelines suggest routine screening for disordered eating in people with Type 1 Diabetes due to elevated risk and associated health complications, it highlights a critical lack of evidence regarding which specific tools are most valid and reliable across different age groups and clinical settings. Consequently, the authors recommend that future research focus on evaluating the validity and reliability of available screening tools by directly comparing them against gold-standard diagnostic interviews to help establish standardized screening guidelines and improve clinical outcomes.
passage_2: "Disordered Eating Behaviors and Eating Disorders in Youth With Type 2 Diabetes: A Systematic Review" evaluates disordered eating behaviors (DEBs) in youth diagnosed with type 2 diabetes by identifying the most common DEBs, analyzing potential risk and protective factors, and reviewing existing screening tools and interventions utilized for this population. Findings indicate that approximately half of the youth study participants had elevated scores on the Diabetes Eating Problem Survey–Revised, showing a higher likelihood of engaging in DEBs compared to youth with type 1 diabetes, with key risk factors including obesity, body weight/shape concerns, and caregiver subclinical binge eating. Recommendations highlight a critical need for further research to construct a framework for understanding influential variables, to advance screening tools, and to design effective targeted interventions.
passage_3: Disturbed Eating Behavior and Omission of Insulin in Adolescents Receiving Intensified Insulin Treatment evaluates the prevalence of disturbed eating behavior (DEB) and insulin restriction or omission among 770 Norwegian adolescents aged 11–19 with type 1 diabetes using the Diabetes Eating Problem Survey-Revised (DEPS-R). The findings indicate that 27.7% of females and 8.6% of males scored above the threshold for DEB, with prevalence increasing significantly alongside higher age and weight categories (reaching 38.1% in the oldest age group and 32.7% among obese participants). Additionally, 31.6% of participants reported restricting insulin and 6.9% reported omitting insulin entirely after overeating. Both DEB and insulin restriction were significantly associated with higher HbA1c levels (9.2% vs. 8.4% for DEB; 9.0% vs. 8.3% for restriction), highlighting poorer metabolic control and elevated risk for long-term diabetes complications. The paper emphasizes the need for early identification and further clinical assessment of at-risk individuals, as well as the importance of early intervention to prevent the development of full-threshold eating disorders and mitigate severe health risks.

passage_1: The study "Systematic Review: Diabetes Family Conflict in Young People With Type 1 Diabetes" evaluates the relationships between diabetes-specific family conflict and various health outcomes—including glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c), treatment adherence, blood glucose monitoring, depression, anxiety, quality of life, and well-being—among young people with type 1 diabetes aged 14 to 25 years. Across 20 included studies, greater diabetes-specific family conflict was significantly associated with higher HbA1c values in 17 studies, suboptimal treatment adherence or less frequent blood glucose monitoring in 7 studies, and poorer quality of life, reduced well-being, or heightened depressive and anxiety symptoms in 7 studies, though 4 studies found no significant links to HbA1c or adherence. Given these findings, the authors recommend routine screening for and intervention addressing diabetes-specific family conflict in clinical practice, while highlighting guidelines for future research to prioritize longitudinal studies specifically targeting young people over the age of 16.
passage_2: The systematic review Screening and identification of disordered eating in people with type 1 diabetes: A systematic review evaluates the reliability, validity, and clinical utility of 48 individual tools used to screen or identify disordered eating behaviors and eating disorders in individuals with Type 1 Diabetes across 90 studies. The authors found that the overall quality of the reported tools was poor, with a high risk of bias stemming from the widespread use of non-validated assessment tools and a lack of comparison against the reference standard of a diagnostic clinical interview. While the review notes that current guidelines suggest routine screening for disordered eating in people with Type 1 Diabetes due to elevated risk and associated health complications, it highlights a critical lack of evidence regarding which specific tools are most valid and reliable across different age groups and clinical settings. Consequently, the authors recommend that future research focus on evaluating the validity and reliability of available screening tools by directly comparing them against gold-standard diagnostic interviews to help establish standardized screening guidelines and improve clinical outcomes.

Weithorn evaluates the role of minors' legal competence in American healthcare decision-making, examining the default doctrine of parental consent alongside statutory and judicial exceptions such as the mature minor doctrine. The analysis finds that a minor's decisional competence is rarely the primary trigger for transferring legal authority; instead, courts and legislatures first assess whether policy goals or constitutional rights justify bypassing parental authority before assessing whether capable minors should decide for themselves. Furthermore, psychological and neuroscientific research indicates that cognitive capacities necessary for logical "cold cognition" reasoning reach adult levels by early to mid-adolescence (around ages 12 to 15), while psychosocial maturity in emotional "hot cognition" contexts continues to develop into adulthood. Based on these findings, the author recommends recognizing that legal authority rules reflect deliberate policy balances rather than simple reflections of developmental maturity, and guidelines emphasize promoting minors' participation as collaborative partners in medical decisions alongside parents and healthcare providers, regardless of strict legal boundaries

Findings indicate that 80% of caregivers and 66% of adolescents logged into a decision aid at least once, spending an average of 55.0 and 46.2 minutes on the website and viewing 72.2% and 77.4% of the content, respectively. Bivariate and regression analyses revealed that non-Hispanic, Caucasian females from higher socioeconomic status households were significantly more likely to log in, while adolescent males with lower health literacy demonstrated fewer logins. Based on these results, the paper recommends that future shared decision-making trials seek to actively promote decision aid engagement—particularly among non-White adolescents, potentially via direct assistance during the initial login—and explicitly guidelines that trials employing electronic decision aids routinely measure, report, and analyze objective utilization data.

question: Did the Youth Involvement in the Decision to Start CGM Predicts Subsequent CGM Use study provide data on long-term adherence beyond 12 weeks?
passage_1: The study Youth Involvement in the Decision to Start CGM Predicts Subsequent CGM Use evaluates whether youth involvement in the decision to initiate continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) influences subsequent CGM adherence, and tests whether CGM self-efficacy and perceived hassle mediate this relationship among parent-youth dyads. The findings reveal that youth involvement in the initial decision positively predicted CGM use between weeks 5 and 12, mediated by the youth perceiving higher self-efficacy and lower hassle at a 2-month follow-up. Based on these findings, the authors recommend that healthcare providers actively facilitate youth participation and input when deciding to initiate CGM therapy in order to maximize long-term device adherence and clinical benefits.
passage_2: Effect of Continuous Glucose Monitoring on Glycemic Control in Adolescents and Young Adults With Type 1 Diabetes: A Randomized Clinical Trial evaluates the impact of continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) compared with standard blood glucose monitoring (BGM) on glycemic control over 26 weeks in 153 adolescents and young adults aged 14 to 24 years with type 1 diabetes. The study found that treatment with CGM resulted in a statistically significant reduction in mean HbA1c levels from 8.9% at baseline to 8.5% at 26 weeks, compared to remaining unchanged at 8.9% in the BGM group (an adjusted between-group difference of -0.37%). Additionally, participants in the CGM group demonstrated improvements in secondary outcomes, including time spent in the target glucose range and reduced daytime and nighttime glucose variability. The study concludes that CGM leads to small but statistically significant improvements in glycemic control in this population and notes that further research is needed to determine the clinical importance and long-term implications of these findings.
passage_3: Early Initiation of Diabetes Devices Relates to Improved Glycemic Control in Children with Recent-Onset Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus evaluates whether initiating an insulin pump or a continuous glucose monitor (CGM) within the first year of diagnosis is associated with reduced glycated hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c) levels in a cohort of 111 children aged 5 to 9 years with recent-onset type 1 diabetes. Tracking participants from baseline (mean diabetes duration of 4.7 months) to a 6-month follow-up (~12 months post-diagnosis), the study found that insulin pump usage grew from 17% to 35.1% and CGM usage increased from 17.1% to 25.2%. The findings demonstrate that children using an insulin pump maintained lower overall HbA1c levels compared to non-users, and children who started using a CGM during this timeframe experienced significantly lower HbA1c levels than those who did not. Based on these findings, the authors conclude and recommend that early initiation of either an insulin pump or a CGM in newly diagnosed children can help improve glycemic control within their first year of living with type 1 diabetes.
